extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers preparing for mathematical olympiads; problem-solvers and coaches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and techniques for creating, organizing, and solving mathematical Olympiad problems (primarily plane geometry, with references to algebra, number theory, and combinatorics). Emphasis on pedagogical organization, common solution techniques, and heuristic criteria for good problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a good Olympiad problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A good Olympiad problem will capture in miniature the process of creating mathematics: immersion in the situation, examination of approaches, pursuit of various paths, dead ends and new perspectives, and the moment of insight; it tells a story of mathematical creativity and leaves the participant wanting more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problems that evoke struggle and insight rather than routine exercises; problems should be nonroutine, open-ended, and illustrate methods that generalize beyond the specific statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization for learning (section structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section treats a particular technique or topic, starts with a short essay discussing basic facts with representative examples, then lists a number of carefully chosen problems, and provides detailed solutions in a second part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange material so introductory results and examples set the tone, problems are self-contained and listed in increasing order of difficulty, and full solutions (with sources) are provided; learners are advised to study solutions even after solving problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coach's central skill: recognizing similarities among problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The craft of a skilled Olympiad coach or teacher consists largely in recognizing similarities among problems; this is the single most important skill a coach can impart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pattern recognition and transfer of methods across problems; cluster problems by common ideas so techniques build to mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rotations for equilateral-triangle constructions (Pompeiu-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: rotate parts of the figure (e.g., rotate by 60° about a vertex in equilateral-triangle problems) to transform lengths/angles and construct auxiliary triangles whose sides equal desired distances (as in Pompeiu’s theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate rotation to convert given distances into sides of a constructed triangle; analyze degeneracy cases (e.g., when the image points are collinear, corresponding to points on the circumcircle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunt for cyclic quadrilaterals when proving angle equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy: when angle equalities are needed, look for cyclic quadrilaterals because cyclicity provides angle relations (Theorem 1: a quadrilateral is cyclic iff one angle equals the supplement of its opposite; Theorem 2: a side–diagonal angle equals the opposite side–other diagonal angle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize patterns like two opposite right angles imply cyclicity; use cyclicity to convert angle statements into equal inscribed angles and derive similarity or congruence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use projections and right-angle constructions to create cyclicity or similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: drop perpendiculars (projections) to sides or tangents to produce right angles; quadrilaterals with two opposite right angles are cyclic and can be used to show triangle similarities or other relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct feet of perpendiculars onto chords/tangents to create cyclic quadrilaterals, then apply inscribed-angle theorems to deduce equal angles and similarity (e.g., to prove mean-geometry relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use directed angles modulo 180° to avoid case-by-case angle-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple configurations/cases arise, work with oriented (directed) angles modulo 180°: take counterclockwise rotations positive, clockwise negative, and identify angles differing by multiples of 180°; four points are concyclic iff directed angle ABC ≡ ADC (mod 180°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt directed-angle conventions to unify many cases and simplify angle algebra; recommend for problems with several possible configurations that look different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of a point as a versatile tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and key property: for a fixed point P and circle, if a line through P meets the circle at A and B then PA·PB is independent of the line (power of P). Power can be expressed as PO^2 − R^2 (directed), and equals the square of the tangent length from P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use power to identify tangency, prove bisector or midpoint properties (via radical axis), compute distances (e.g., Euler relation OI^2 = R(R − 2r)), and reduce locus problems to linear relations (radical axis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical axis and radical center properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The locus of points with equal powers w.r.t. two circles is a line perpendicular to the line of centers (the radical axis). For three circles with noncollinear centers, pairwise radical axes concur at the radical center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use radical-axis intersections and common-tangent midpoints to locate special points; apply concurrency of radical axes in configuration proofs and to show midpoints of common tangents or concurrency properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive length relations via similarity from cyclic/symmetric constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: obtain triangle similarity from cyclic/quadrilateral properties (or right-angle constructions) to translate angle equalities into proportional segment relations, enabling product or mean relations (e.g., showing PQ^2 = PR·PS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up similar triangles by identifying equal inscribed or vertical angles; then equate ratios to prove multiplicative or additive relations among segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer elementary/geometric methods but allow occasional use of higher tools sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The book places problems just beyond the usual high-school curriculum and sometimes refers to calculus, vectors, matrices, but these are rarely relied on; solutions emphasize elementary, imaginative geometric or algebraic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor synthetic geometric transformations (rotations, reflections, inversion, homothety), elementary inequalities and classical results; avoid over-reliance on heavy machinery unless it simplifies the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical practice: list problems in increasing difficulty and include sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are generally listed in increasing order of difficulty; solutions to all problems are given in detail with sources when known, and sections are self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use earlier, simpler problems to suggest ideas for harder ones; teachers should assign representative examples and encourage students to read official solutions even after solving a problem to learn alternative approaches.
